rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thaʿlabī identifies Ezra as the traveler who escaped Babylon, reached an abandoned village, ate its fruit and drank its grape juice, then wondered how God could revive it after death.
rows.anchor: فلما نجا عزير من بابل ارتحل على حمار حتى نزل على دير هرقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ezra's question about reviving the village expressed amazement, not doubt in resurrection.
rows.anchor: لم يشك في البعث ولكن قالها تعجبا

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb's account says Jeremiah tied his donkey, then God put him to sleep, took his soul for a hundred years, and killed the donkey while preserving its food and drink.
rows.anchor: قال: ربط أرميا حماره بحبل جديد فألقى الله عليه النوم، فلما نام نزع منه الروح

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: In Wahb's report, God concealed Jeremiah from sight and kept beasts and birds from eating his body.
rows.anchor: وأعمى الله عنه العيون فلم يره أحد وذلك ضحى

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: After seventy years God ordered a king to rebuild Jerusalem and its surroundings; a thousand stewards each led three hundred thousand workers, and the city was rebuilt over thirty years.
rows.anchor: فلما مضى من موته سبعون سنة أرسل الله عز وجل ملكا

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb's account says God destroyed Nebuchadnezzar with a mosquito and returned surviving Israelites from Babylon to Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وأهلك الله تعالى بخت نصر ببعوضة دخلت دماغه

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: At the hundred-year mark God revived Jeremiah's eyes and then body; he watched the donkey's scattered bones gather, receive flesh and skin, and revive.
rows.anchor: فلما مضت المائة أحيا الله تعالى منه عينيه وسائر جسده ميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thaʿlabī says God restored Jeremiah to life; this is the event described by the verse's statement that God made him die for a hundred years and then raised him.
rows.anchor: وعمر الله أرميا، فهو الذي يرى في الفلوات فذلك قوله تعالى: فأماته الله مائة عام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative kam asks for the amount of time he remained there.
rows.anchor: قال كم استفهام عن مبلغ العدد لبثت

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن والأعمش وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers assimilate the thāʾ in labith and labithtum throughout the Qurʾan; the remaining readers pronounce it distinctly.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن محيص والأعمش وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي: لبث ولبثم بالإدغام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation is based on closeness of articulation and similarity in whispering; distinct pronunciation follows the written form. Both readings are eloquent, and labitha means to stay or reside.
rows.anchor: وكلاهما غريبان فصيحان ومعناه: كم مكثت وأقمت هاهنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God caused him to die at midday and revived him a hundred years later near sunset, so he first thought a day had passed, then corrected himself to part of a day when he saw sunlight remaining.
rows.anchor: أماته ضحى في أول النهار وأحياه بعد مائة عام في آخر النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle aw signals a retraction from saying one day, as in the expression aw yazidun.
rows.anchor: فقال: أو بعض يوم بمعنى بل بعض يوم، لأن قوله بعض يوم رجوع عن قوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food was figs and the drink grape juice; they had not changed over the years.
rows.anchor: فانظر إلى طعامك يعني التين وشرابك يعني العصير لم يتسنه

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisāʾī omit the hāʾ of yat asannah in connected recitation, as they do in fa-bihudāhumuqtadih; the other readers retain it in pause and connection.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي بحذف الهاء وصلا وكذلك في قوله

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم عن طلحة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim reports Ṭalḥa's assimilation of the tāʾ into the sīn and says this reading is also found in Ubayy's codex; the meaning is that years did not alter the food.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو حاتم عن طلحة لم يتسنه بإدغام التاء في السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One morphological analysis treats the hāʾ as an added pause-link: the original form is yasna, with yāʾ removed by jussive marking and hāʾ supplied at pause.
rows.anchor: أصله لم يتسنى فحذف الياء بالجزم وأبدل منها هاء في الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the view that the hāʾ is added, sanah has a wāw root and plural sanawāt; its verb forms include sāniya and tasannā.
rows.anchor: وهذا على قول من جعل الهاء في السنة زائدة.

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr derives the word from tasannun, meaning change, as in the description of altered mud as hamāʾ masnūn.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمر: وهو من التسنن بنونين، وهو التغيير كقوله: من حمإ مسنون

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A cited line uses al-taʿayyun as a witness for the relevant derivational pattern; the text explains that the poet intended that form.
rows.anchor: فهلا إذ سمعت بحثت عنه … ولم تمس الحكومة بالتظني

rows.speaker: العجاج
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj's line is cited as an example of a form with an intended doubled letter, parallel to the word's derivation.
rows.anchor: قال العجاج: تفصي البازي إذ البازي كسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic expression natalaʿā describes people going out to gather a tender plant called al-maqāʿ; the verse also cites daṣṣāhā for dassasahā.
rows.anchor: وتقول العرب: نتلعى، إذا خرجوا في اجتناء نبت ناعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers who retain the hāʾ in both positions treat it as a root letter; on this account the word is sanhiyah, diminutive sunayhah, with the verb musāhanah.
rows.anchor: ومن أثبت الهاء في الحالين جعلها هاء أصلية لام الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse mentions two items, the verb's change concerns the nearer word, the years; the other item is omitted as understood. Ibn Masʿūd's reading explicitly repeats the drink.
rows.anchor: لأن التغيير راجع إلى أقرب اللفظين وهو السنوات، واكتفى بذكر أحد المذكورين

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd's reading says, “look at your food and this drink; it has not changed,” supporting the explanation of the singular verb.
rows.anchor: ودليل هذا التأويل قراءة ابن مسعود: فانظر إلى طعامك وهذا شرابك لم يتسنه.

rows.speaker: أكثر العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars take the verse as fronting and postponing its clauses: first look at the unchanged food and drink, then at the donkey; another possible reading leaves the sequence straightforward.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر العلماء: في الآية تقديم وتأخير، أي وانظر إلى طعامك

rows.speaker: خارجة والأعرج وعيسى بن عمر وابن عامر وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers incline the vowel in ḥimār and al-ḥimār; the remaining readers use the full, non-imālah pronunciation.
rows.anchor: قرأ خارجة والأعرج وعيسى بن عمر وابن عامر وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب وعبد الله بن عامر والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: These readers pronounce nunshizuhā with zāy, a ḍamma on the nūn, and kasra on the shīn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبي بن كعب وعبد الله بن عامر والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وخلف

rows.speaker: أبو العالية عن زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya reports Zayd ibn Thābit saying that the letter is actually rāʾ and readers merely dotted it as zāy; a parallel report from Ibn ʿAbbās is cited and Abū ʿUbayda prefers zāy.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو العالية عن زيد بن ثابت قال: إنما هي راء قرؤها زاء أي أنقطها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zāy reading means raising and moving the bones back to their bodily positions, assembling them together.
rows.anchor: وانشاز الشيء: رفعه ونقله وإزعاجه، فقال: أنشزته فنشز، أي رفعته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī explain the verb as bringing the bones out; al-Kisāʾī explains it as making them grow and become large.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والسدي: نخرجها، والكسائي: فننبتها ونعظمها.

rows.speaker: قتادة وعطاء وأبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب وأيوب
rows.claim: These readers use nunshiru with rāʾ, meaning “revive”; Abū Ḥātim chooses this reading.
rows.anchor: قتادة وعطاء وأبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rāʾ reading means that God revives the dead; Thaʿlabī links it to several Qurʾanic uses of nashara and nushūr.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: نحييها. فقال: أنشر الله الميت إنشارا فينشر هو نشورا، قال الله تعالى:

rows.speaker: حارثة بن بدر الغداني
rows.claim: Ḥāritha ibn Badr al-Ghadānī's verse uses anshara for reviving the dead and restoring their minds.
rows.anchor: وقال حارثة بن بدر الغداني:

rows.speaker: الحسن والمفضل
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and al-Mufaḍḍal read nunshuruhā with rāʾ, fatḥa on nūn and ḍamma on shīn; al-Farrāʾ relates it to spreading and folding.
rows.anchor: قرأ الحسن والمفضل ننشرها بالراء وفتح النون وضم الشين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say this reading also means reviving; Abū Ḥātim says that usage is not familiar.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حاتم: وليس بالمعروف.

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī reads nunshizuhā with zāy and fatḥa on nūn; Abū Ḥātim calls it an error, while others treat nashazahu and anshazahu as synonymous.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النخعي بالزاء وفتح النون وضم الشين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then We cover them with flesh” compares covering the bones with flesh to covering a body with clothing.
rows.anchor: أي نكسوها ونواريها به كما نواري الجسد بالثوب

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators understand the bones to be the donkey's, which God had killed and then restored whole while the man watched.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: أراد به عظام حماره وذلك أن الله تعالى أمات حماره

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī reports that God revived Ezra while the donkey's bones were scattered; a wind gathered and fitted them, flesh and blood covered them, and an angel blew into its nostrils so it rose and brayed.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: إن الله أحيا عزيرا ثم قال انظر إلى حمارك قد هلك وبليت عظامه

rows.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة والربيع وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ, and Ibn Zayd say the bones are the man's: God revived his eyes while his body was dead, and his donkey remained alive as before.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الضحاك وقتادة والربيع وابن زيد

rows.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة والربيع وابن زيد
rows.claim: On this interpretation, the omitted phrase is “look at your bones”; the donkey stood as it had when tied, and its neck amulet remained new after a hundred years.
rows.anchor: وتقدير الآية على هذا القول: فانظر إلى حمارك وانظر إلى عظامك كيف ننشزها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “and to make you a sign for people” explains the purpose of the event; the next segment develops its meaning.
rows.anchor: ولنجعلك آية للناس فعلنا ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line by al-Aswad ibn Jaʿfar illustrates the interpretation of the conjunction as an extra wāw by using fa-idha dhalika to mean “when that happened.”
rows.anchor: فإذا وذلك لا مهاة لذكره … والدهر يعقب صالحا بفساد

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators say the event made him a sign, lesson, and proof of resurrection after death.
rows.anchor: أي عبرة ودلالة على البعث بعد الموت، قاله أكثر المفسرين.

rows.speaker: الضحاك وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others say the sign was that he returned to his village young, with black hair and beard, while his children and grandchildren had become old.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك وغيره: هذه الآية أنه عاد إلى قريته شابا

rows.speaker: قتادة عن كعب والحسن ومقاتل وجويبر عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس وعبد الله بن إسماعيل السدي عن أبيه عن مجاهد عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says the revived Ezra rode home, failed to recognize the village, and found his former blind, paralyzed servant, now 120, who asked him to restore her sight and mobility.
rows.anchor: لما أحيا الله عزيرا بعد ما أماته مائة سنة ركب حماره حتى أتى محلته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ezra prayed and touched the woman's eyes; her sight and legs were restored and she recognized him.
rows.anchor: فدعا ربه ومسح يده على عينيها ففتحت وأخذ بيدها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The woman called the people together, including Ezra's aged son and grandsons; at first they disbelieved her claim that Ezra had returned.
rows.anchor: فنادت: هذا عزير قد جاءكم، فكذبوها.

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
rows.claim: These authorities say Ezra's son recognized him by a black, crescent-shaped mark between his shoulders.
rows.anchor: كانت لأبي شامة سوداء مثل الهلال بين كتفيه

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
rows.claim: They report that after Nebuchadnezzar burned the Torah, an angel gave Ezra water and God inscribed the Torah in his chest and sent him as a prophet.
rows.anchor: فأتاه ملك بإناء فيه ماء فسقاه من ذلك الإناء فمثلت التوراة في صدره

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
rows.claim: Ezra dictated the Torah from memory; a man retrieved a copy buried in his grandfather's vineyard, and the two texts matched letter for letter.
rows.anchor: فأملاها عليهم من ظهر قلبه

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
rows.claim: They say the Israelites then called Ezra God's son because they thought no one could possess the Torah after its loss unless he were God's son.
rows.anchor: فعندها قالوا: عزير ابن الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو رجاء وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers connect qāla aʿlam as a jussive command, with God telling him “know”; ʿAbd Allāh and al-Aʿmash read qul aʿlam to support this.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عباس وأبو رجاء وحمزة والكسائي: قال أعلم موصولا مجزوما على الأمر

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers take qāla aʿlam as a declarative report that Ezra said he now knew God could do all things.
rows.anchor: قرأ الباقون قال أعلم معطوفا مرفوعا على الخبر عن عزير

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb reports that Paradise has no dogs or donkeys except the dog of the Cave Companions and Jeremiah's donkey.
rows.anchor: عن المنعم بن إدريس عن أبيه عن وهب قال: ليس في الجنة كلب ولا حمار إلا كلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's compressed comparison means the likeness of the charity of those who spend in God's path; alternatively, it compares the spenders themselves to a farmer sowing a seed.
rows.anchor: الآية فيها إضمار واختصار تقديرها: مثل صدقات الذين ينفقون أموالهم، فإن شئت

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وأبو غزية وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers assimilate the tāʾ in sanābil to the following sīn; others pronounce the two words distinctly, the common language.
rows.anchor: أدغمها أبو عمرو أبو [غزية] وحمزة والكسائي، وأظهرها الباقون.

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr cites a line that turns sīn into tāʾ, with al-nāt intended to mean al-nās, as evidence for assimilation.
rows.anchor: أنشد أبو عمرو: يا لعن الله بني السعلاة … عمرو بن ميمون لئام النات

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر والأعمش
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and al-Aʿmash shorten the readings of khams miʾah and miʾah; the other readers lengthen them.
rows.anchor: أبو جعفر والأعمش: يتركان خمس مائة ومائة، حيث كانت استخفافا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thaʿlabī says a spike with a hundred grains is not impossible; if none is observed, the comparison can mean one planted seed produces seven spikes of a hundred grains apiece.
rows.anchor: لا ننكر ذلك ولا يستحيل، فإن يكن موجودا فهو ذلك وإلا فجائز أن يكون

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says that every spike produced a hundred grains.
rows.anchor: وكذلك ما قاله الضحاك قال: أنبتت كل سنبلة مائة حبة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may multiply the reward from seven to seventy or seven hundred and beyond, to an amount known only to God.
rows.anchor: والله يضاعف لمن يشاء ما بين سبع وسبعين وسبعمائة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is ample in the reward multiples and knows who spends.
rows.anchor: والله واسع غني لتلك الأضعاف عليم بمن ينفق

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says a person who gives one dirham seeking God's pleasure receives seven hundred dirhams in immediate worldly replacement and meets a thousand on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك في هذه الآية: من أخرج درهما [ابتغاء] مرضاة الله فله في الدنيا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the verse was revealed about ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf: the latter gave four thousand dirhams and kept four thousand for his family; the Prophet blessed both parts.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي في قوله الذين ينفقون أموالهم في سبيل الله الآية: نزلت في عثمان بن عفان

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The same occasion report says ʿUthmān equipped a thousand camels for the Tabūk expedition and donated the well of Rumah to Muslims.
rows.anchor: فجهز المسلمين ألف بعير بأحلاسها وأقتابها وتصدق برومة ركية

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن سمرة
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samura reports that ʿUthmān brought a thousand dinars for the army of hardship, and the Prophet praised what he had done.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الرحمن بن سمرة: جاء عثمان (رضي الله عنه) بألف دينار في جيش العسرة

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī says he saw the Prophet pray for ʿUthmān until dawn, after which the verse was revealed about him.
rows.anchor: قال أبو سعيد الخدري: رأيت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رافعا يده يدعو لعثمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following a gift with mann means reminding its recipient of it, recounting favors, or repeatedly making the gift a reproach; the root first meant to bestow.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يمن عليه بعطائه ويعد نعمه عليه يكدرها يواصل المنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man derives from giving or bestowing; the word came to mean recalling and claiming credit for a favor.
rows.anchor: يقال: من يمن منة ومنا ومنية إذا أنعم وأعطى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Harm includes publicizing a gift to someone who need not know of it and other hurtful speech.
rows.anchor: بإظهار العطية وذكرها لمن لا يجب وقوفه عليها

rows.speaker: سفيان والمفضل
rows.claim: Sufyān and al-Mufaḍḍal explain mann and harm as saying, “I gave you, but you did not thank me.”
rows.anchor: قال سفيان والمفضل في قوله: منا ولا أذى: هو أن يقول أعطيتك فما شكرت.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it is better not to give than to give and then follow the gift with reproach and harm.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: أن لا ينفق الرجل ماله خير من أن ينفقه ثم يتبعه منا وأذى.

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd reports his father advising donors to withhold even a greeting if they think it will burden the recipient.
rows.anchor: إذا أعطيت رجلا شيئا وظننت أن سلامك يثقل عليه

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd recounts that his father rebuked a woman who suspected men going to jihad only wanted fruit; her words had hurt them before she gave them a quiver and arrows.
rows.anchor: فقد أذيتهم قبل أن تعطيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reserves mann as an attribute of grace: human reminders taunt and spoil a gift, whereas God's mention of a blessing is beneficence and favor.
rows.anchor: فحظر الله عن عباده المن بالصنيعة وأختص به صفتا لنفسه

rows.speaker: معاد بن المثنى عن أبيه محمود بن الوراق
rows.claim: A poem attributed to Maʿād ibn al-Muthannā, from his father Maḥmūd ibn al-Warrāq, praises a good deed free from reproach.
rows.anchor: وأنشد معاد بن المثنى العنبري عن أبيه محمود بن الوراق: أحسن من كل حسن

rows.speaker: أبو ذر القرطبي
rows.claim: A poem transmitted by Abū Dharr al-Qurṭubī warns that reminding people of a favor diminishes it and spoils the giver's generosity.
rows.anchor: قال الثعلبي: أبو علي زاهر بن أحمد السرخسي قال: أنشدنا أبو ذر القرطبي:

rows.speaker: محمد بن طاهر عن أبي علي البصري
rows.claim: A poem describes a recipient turning hostile to a benefactor when the benefactor's fortunes later decline.
rows.anchor: قال: وأنشدني محمد بن القاسم قال: أنشدني محمد بن طاهر قال: أنشدني أبو علي البصري:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another poem says that reproach ruins the good already done and that a generous person does not remind others of gifts.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: أفسدت بالمن ما قدمت من حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kind, gracious answer to a petitioner is “known good”; al-Kalbī defines it as a sincere prayer for one's brother in his absence, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk as speech reconciling people.
rows.anchor: قول معروف أي كلام حسن ورد على السائل جميل

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Jarīr explains forgiveness as the donor's overlooking the poor person's need-related conduct; al-Kalbī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also call it pardon for an insult.
rows.anchor: ومغفرة أي مغفرة منه عليه لما علم خلته وفاقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because a poor person may be distressed by refusal and answer harshly or complain, the giver is urged to pardon him; this is better than a gift followed by harm.
rows.anchor: فحثه على الصفح والعفو وبين أن ذلك خير له من صدقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Harm after charity includes reproaching the petitioner for asking, complaining about him, finding fault, or other hurtful remarks.
rows.anchor: من وتعيير السائل بالسؤال أو شكاية منه أو عيب أو قول يؤذيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no need of human charity; He could enrich everyone, but gave wealth to test the rich in gratitude and left the poor to be tested in patience.
rows.anchor: ولو شاء لأغنى جميع الخلق ولكنه أعطى الأغنياء لينظر كيف شكرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is forbearing because He does not hasten punishment for someone who reproaches or harms with a gift.
rows.anchor: حليم إذ لم يعجل على من يمن ويؤذي بصدقته

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمان السليماني
rows.claim: A report from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulaymānī, client of ʿUmar, attributes to the Prophet advice not to interrupt a petitioner and to answer with dignity, gentleness, a small gift, or gracious refusal.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إذا سأل السائل فلا تقطعوا عليه مسألته

rows.speaker: بشر بن الحرث
rows.claim: Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith recounts a dream in which ʿAlī said that a poor person's confidence in God is even better than a rich person's charitable kindness.
rows.anchor: وأحسن منه تيه الفقراء على الأغنياء ثقة بالله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition means not to erase charity's reward and the reward of spending by reproaching the recipient.
rows.anchor: أي لا تحبطوا أجور صدقاتكم وثواب نفقاتكم بالمن على السائل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the reproach is toward God and the harm is toward the recipient.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بالمن على الله تعالى والأذى لصاحبها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison is to a hypocrite who spends for show, since an openly unbelieving person would not pretend to give for public praise.
rows.anchor: وهذا للمنافقين لأن الكافر معلن كفره غير مرائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣafwān is a smooth, bare stone; a cited poem evokes planting gravel on a smooth expanse of ground.
rows.anchor: كمثل صفوان الحجر إلا ملس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ṣafwān is treated as a collective, its singular is ṣafwānah, like tamrah from tamr and nakhlah from nakhl.
rows.anchor: وهو واحد وجمع، فمن جعله جمعا قال: واحده صفوانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the view that ṣafwān is singular, its plural is ṣafī or ṣafā.
rows.anchor: ومن جعله واحدا قال: جمعه صفي وصفى.

rows.speaker: الزعري
rows.claim: Al-Zaʿrī vocalizes ṣafwān with fatḥa and says its plural remains ṣafwān, like karawān and warshān.
rows.anchor: وقال الزعري: صفوان بفتح الفاء، وجمعه صفوان مثل كروان وكروان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wābil is heavy rain; ṣald is hard, smooth stone with nothing on it, as in the cited line by Ṭaʾabbaṭa Sharrā.
rows.anchor: وابل وهو المطر الشديد العظيم القطر فتركه صلدا وهو الحجر الصلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṣald also describes infertile land or a head without hair; a line by Ruʾbah illustrates the latter sense.
rows.anchor: وهو من الأرض ما لا ينبت، ومن الرؤوس ما لا شعر عليه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stone parable depicts the apparent good deeds of hypocrites, show-offs, and donors who reproach or harm: judgment makes the work vanish because it was not done for God.
rows.anchor: وهذا مثل ضربه الله تعالى لنفقة المنافق والمرائي والمؤمن الذي يمن بصدقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thaʿlabī compares the parable with the Qurʾanic images of unbelievers' deeds as windblown ashes and as a mirage.
rows.anchor: نظيره قوله تعالى في وصف أعمال الكفار: مثل الذين كفروا بربهم أعمالهم كرماد اشتدت به الريح

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿIkrimah reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that a caller will tell those who acted to be seen by people to collect their wages from those for whom they acted, since God accepts no work mixed with worldly aims.
rows.anchor: عكرمة عن ابن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «إذا كان يوم القيامة نادى مناد

rows.speaker: عبد الله المدني
rows.claim: A report relayed by ʿAbd Allāh al-Madanī introduces a man who heard Abū Hurayrah narrate the Prophet's warning and asks him to explain his repeated tears.
rows.anchor: عبد الله المدني قال: بلغني أن رجلا دخل على معاوية قال: مررت بالمدينة فإذا أبو هريرة جالس

rows.speaker: عبد الله المدني
rows.claim: In the continuation of the report, the wealthy man says he spent to be called generous; the Prophet's account says the praise he sought was already given but earns him nothing.
rows.anchor: أردت أن يقال فلان سخي فقد قيل لك فماذا يغني عنك

rows.speaker: عبد الله المدني
rows.claim: The report says a warrior fought to be called brave and a scholar learned and taught to be called learned; both are condemned for seeking reputation.
rows.anchor: أردت أن يقال فلان عالم وقد قيل فماذا يغني عنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking God's pleasure means desiring His approval; “stabilizing themselves” has several interpretations reported below.
rows.anchor: ابتغاء مرضات الله طلب رضا الله وتثبيتا من أنفسهم

rows.speaker: الشعبي والكلبي والضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Jalabī, al-Kalbī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk take tathbīt as affirmation: donors give zakat willingly, knowing what they spend is better for them than what they keep.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي والكلبي والضحاك: يعني تصديقا من أنفسهم يخرجون الزكاة طيبة بها أنفسهم

rows.speaker: السدي وأبو صالح وأبو روق وابن زيد والمفضل
rows.claim: These authorities explain tathbīt as certainty that God will replace what they spend.
rows.anchor: السدي وأبو صالح وأبو روق وابن زيد والمفضل: على يقين إخلاف الله عليهم.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains it as seeking reward in faith.
rows.anchor: قتادة: احتسابا بإيمان من أنفسهم، عطاء ومجاهد:

rows.speaker: عطاء ومجاهد
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and Mujāhid say the donors are assured they will not lose their wealth; Mujāhid's reading says “for their own selves.”
rows.anchor: عطاء ومجاهد: مثبتون أي لا يضيعون أموالهم، وكذلك قرأ مجاهد:

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says a person considering charity deliberates: if it is for God, he gives, but if another motive is mixed in, he holds back; tathbīt here means deliberation.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: كان الرجل إذا هم بصدقة تثبت إن كان لله أعطى

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وأبو مالك
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Abū Mālik interpret the phrase as lessening their sin.
rows.anchor: سعيد بن جبير وأبو مالك: تخفيفا في ذنبهم.

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysān reads the phrase as sincerity and habituating themselves to obey God in their spending.
rows.anchor: ابن كيسان: إخلاصا وتوطينا لأنفسهم على طاعة الله عز وجل في نفقاتهم،

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says they spend while acknowledging that God watches them.
rows.anchor: الزجاج: ينفقونها مقرين بأن الله عز وجل رقيب عليهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of tathbīt is to make something firm: the expression describes someone who verifies an undertaking, persists in it, and strengthens himself to do it; a poem illustrates the word.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذه الكلمة من قول السائل: ثبت فلان في هذا الأمر إذا حققه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says a garden with date palms is called jannah, whereas a vineyard is called firdaws.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: إذا كان في البستان نخل فهو جنة، وإذا كان كرم فهو فردوس.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid is cited for reading the comparison as like a seed, and the segment begins reporting regional readings of rabwah.
rows.anchor: وقول مجاهد: كمثل حبة بالحاء والباء بربوة

rows.speaker: السليمي والعطاردي والحسن وعاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers pronounce rabwah with fatḥa on the rāʾ in this verse and in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn; the source calls it the Banū Tamīm dialect.
rows.anchor: قرأ السليمي والعطاردي والحسن وعاصم وابن عامر: بربوة بفتح الراء هاهنا

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وابن كثير والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وخلف وأبو عمرو ويعقوب وأيوب
rows.claim: These readers pronounce rabwah with ḍamma on rāʾ in both places; Abū Ḥātim and Abū ʿUbayd prefer it as the fullest and best-known language.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وابن كثير والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي

rows.speaker: أشهب العقيلي
rows.claim: Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī reads rabāwah with an added alif and kasra on rāʾ; all readings mean level elevated land with flowing water.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أشهب العقيلي: برباوة بالألف وكسر الراء فيها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raised ground is called rabwah because it rises and grows; plants flourish there, and its land is level and supplied with water.
rows.anchor: وهي جميعا المكان المرتفع المستوي الذي تجري فيه الأنهار

rows.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr read akulahā with a light kāf; the other readers double it, and the word means fruit.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو: أكلها بالتخفيف والباقون بالتشديد

rows.speaker: المفضل
rows.claim: Al-Mufaḍḍal defines akl as the abundance and quality of what strengthens something, like a garment containing much yarn; here the garden gives double fruit.
rows.anchor: قال المفضل: الأكل: كثرة ما في الشيء مما يجود ويقوى به

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says the garden produced in one year what another garden produced in two.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء: حملت في سنة من الريع ما تحمل غيرها في سنتين.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrimah says the garden yielded twice in one year.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: حملت في السنة مرتين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭall means light, gentle rain; al-Suddī identifies it as dew.
rows.anchor: فطل أي فطش وهو أضعف المطر وألينه

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the comparison is Egyptian land, which grows well without rain but weakens when rain falls; likewise sincere charity earns multiplied reward whether small or large, without reproach or harm.
rows.anchor: وهذا مثل ضربه الله عز وجل لعمل المؤمن المخلص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden parable in 2:266 connects back to the prohibition on nullifying charity with reproach and harm.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية متصلة بقوله تعالى: يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تبطلوا صدقاتكم بالمن والأذى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past verb aṣābahu follows a future construction because Arabic permits widad with either past-like law or future-like an; they can be interchanged in this sense.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال: أصابه فرد الماضي على المستقبل لأن العرب تلفظ توددت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because law and an may substitute for each other after wishing, aṣābahā is understood as a future event, even though it is expressed in the past; a line of poetry illustrates the construction.
rows.anchor: فلما جاز ذلك صلح أن يقال: فعل بتأويل يفعل ويفعل بتأويل فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable's owner is old and has weak, helpless young children; an iʿṣār is a rising whirlwind like a column, and its plural is aʿāṣīr.
rows.anchor: وأصابه الكبر وله ذرية أولاد صغار ضعفاء عجزة فأصابها إعصار

rows.speaker: الكميت
rows.claim: Al-Kumayt's lines use iʿṣār for a forceful, dust-bearing whirlwind, as a lexical witness.
rows.anchor: بالسافيات وفي غربال إعصار

rows.speaker: يزيد بن المقرع الحميري
rows.claim: Yazīd ibn al-Muqriʿ al-Ḥimyarī uses the plural aʿāṣīr in a poem as further evidence for the word.
rows.anchor: أناس أجارونا وكان جوارهم … أعاصير من فسو العراق المبذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable depicts a hypocritical show-off who expects benefit from his work, but loses it in old age when he and his helpless children cannot restore the burned garden; so the work is voided when repentance is no longer possible.
rows.anchor: وهذا مثل ضربه الله تعالى لنفقة المنافق المرائي

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr instead applies the parable to someone who begins with righteous work, later persists in evil, and dies in that state; the fire-filled whirlwind represents the final evil.
rows.anchor: ضربت مثلا للعمل يبدأ فيعمل عملا صالحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Good things” means the choice and finest portions of what one has earned, in line with the command to spend what one loves.
rows.anchor: تصدقوا من طيبات خيار وجياد نظير قوله: لن تنالوا البر حتى تنفقوا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid interpret ṭayyibāt here as lawful goods, supported by the commands to the messengers and believers to eat from the good things.
rows.anchor: ابن مسعود ومجاهد: حلالات، دليله قوله: يا أيها الرسل كلوا من الطيبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse addressed to believers to eat from the good provisions supports interpreting ṭayyibāt as lawful, good earnings.
rows.anchor: يا أيها الذين آمنوا كلوا من طيبات ما رزقناكم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report says God accepts only what is good: charity from unlawful wealth is not accepted, its owner is not blessed by spending it, and it becomes provision for Hell; evil is not erased by evil.
rows.anchor: وإن الله طيب لا يقبل إلا طيبا، لا يكسب عبد مالا من حرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What you have earned” includes wealth made through trade and craft, such as gold and silver.
rows.anchor: ما كسبتم بالتجارة والصناعة من الذهب والفضة

rows.speaker: عبيد بن رفاعة
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn Rifāʿah reports the Prophet calling merchants sinful except those who are pious, dutiful, and truthful.
rows.anchor: قال عبيد بن رفاعة: خرج علينا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال: «يا معشر التجار أنتم فجار

rows.speaker: قيس بن عروة الغفاري
rows.claim: Qays ibn ʿUrwah al-Ghifārī says the Prophet renamed brokers as traders and told them to offset the distractions, lies, and oaths of selling with charity.
rows.anchor: وقال قيس بن عروة الغفاري: كنا على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بالمدينة

rows.speaker: مكحول عن أبي أمامة
rows.claim: Makhūl reports from Abū Umāmah a saying that trade is the best of ten shares of livelihood when the trader gives and takes what is right, and another report says nine tenths of provision is in trade.
rows.anchor: الخير عشرة أجزاء أفضلها التجارة إذا أخذ الحق وأعطاه

rows.speaker: ابن جريج عن عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās urges Quraysh not to let their non-Arab clients surpass them in trade, praises its blessing, and warns against an oath-swearing, base merchant.
rows.anchor: يا معشر قريش لا يغلبنكم هذه الموالي على التجارة

rows.speaker: عاصم ابن أبي النجود عن أبي وائل
rows.claim: Abū Wāʾil says a dirham earned in trade is dearer to him than ten dirhams from his stipend.
rows.anchor: درهم من تجارة أحب إلي من عشرة من عطائي

rows.speaker: الأعمش عن أبي إبراهيم عن عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports the Prophet saying that the best food a man eats comes from his own earnings, and his child is part of his earnings.
rows.anchor: أطيب ما أكل الرجل من كسبه وإن ولده من كسبه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn ʿUmayr reports that the best livelihood is a man's work by his own hand and every fair sale.
rows.anchor: عمل الرجل بيده وكل بيع مبرور

rows.speaker: محمد بن الراضبي
rows.claim: Muḥammad al-Rāḍibī recounts Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī saying that spinning is among good provisions, citing ʿAlī.
rows.anchor: إنه من طيبات الرزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Produce from the earth means staple, storable grains and fruits on which zakat is due.
rows.anchor: يعني الحبوب والثمار التي تقتات وتدخر مما يجب فيه الزكاة

rows.speaker: عمر بن دينار عن جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jābir reports that the Prophet said whoever plants a tree receives charity for every person, animal, or bird that eats from it until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: فلا يغرس المسلم غرسا فيأكل منه إنسان ولا دابة ولا طائر

rows.speaker: هشام بن عروة عن أبيه عن عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports the Prophet advising people to seek provision in the hidden places of the earth.
rows.anchor: قال التمسوا الرزق في خبايا الأرض

rows.speaker: مالك بن دينار
rows.claim: Mālik ibn Dīnār says he read in the Torah a blessing for one who eats the fruit of his own hands.
rows.anchor: قال مالك بن دينار: قرأت في التوراة: طوبى لمن أكل من ثمرة يديه.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the command with hamza as taʾammamū; Ibn ʿAbbās reads it with a different vowel pattern, both meaning “aim for.”
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن مسعود: ولا تأمموا بالهمز. وقرأ ابن عباس: ولا تيمموا مضمومة التاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr doubles the yāʾ in tayammamū at this and thirty other places, contracting the original two tāʾs; other readers use the light form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير: (ولا تيمموا) بتشديد الياء وفتحها فيها وفي أخواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms amamtu, tayammamtu, and taʾammamtu all mean to intend or aim; a line by al-Aʿshā witnesses tayammamtu.
rows.anchor: وهي كلها لغات بمعنى واحد، يقال: أممت فلانا وتيممته وتأممته، إذا قصدته

rows.speaker: السدي عن علي بن ثابت عن الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reports that the verse addressed Anṣār who hung date clusters in the Prophet's mosque for poor emigrants; some chose clusters of rotten dates, thinking the abundance excused it.
rows.anchor: نزلت هذه الآية في الأنصار كانت تخرج إذا كان جذاذ النخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bad gift is a cluster containing rotten dates, which the giver would not accept if it were offered to him.
rows.anchor: يعني القنو الذي فيه الحشف ولو كان أهدى لكم ما قبلتموه

rows.speaker: باذان عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports the Prophet saying that God has a due in people's property, to be paid when it reaches the required amount; people brought charity to the mosque for him to distribute.
rows.anchor: إن لله في أموالكم حقا فإذا بلغ حق الله في أموالكم فأعطوا منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says a man placed a cluster of rotten dates into the charity after worshippers had dispersed; the Prophet condemned the donor, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: فلما خرج رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبصره فقال: «من جاء بهذا العذق الحشف»

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن ومجاهد والضحاك
rows.claim: ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say people gave the worst of their fruit and property while keeping the good; examples include rotten dates, spoiled grain, and debased coins.
rows.anchor: كانوا يتصدقون بشرار ثمارهم ورذالة أموالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax of illa an tughmiḍū fīhi has an omitted preposition and means “unless you overlook it.”
rows.anchor: ولستم بآخذيه إلا أن تغمضوا فيه محل أن نصب بنزع حرف الصفة، يعني: بأن تغمضوا فيه.

rows.speaker: الزهري والحسن وقتادة وأبو مجلن
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and Abū Mujlaz transmit different vowelings of tughmiḍū; the readings represent recognized dialect forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري: تغمضوا بفتح التاء وضم الميم. وقرأ الحسن بفتح التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ighmāḍ literally means lowering the gaze or closing one eyelid over the other, then came to mean tolerating or relaxing one's standards in a sale.
rows.anchor: والإغماض: غض البصر وإطباق جفن على جفن.

rows.speaker: علي والبراء بن عازب
rows.claim: ʿAlī and al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib explain the verse as a creditor's reluctance to accept an inferior item except by overlooking part of his right; al-ʿAwfī transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: قال علي والبراء بن عازب: معناه: لو كان لأحدكم على رجل حق فجاءه بهذا

rows.speaker: الولبي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Wālibī reports Ibn ʿAbbās explaining that one would not accept the poor item at the value of good produce without reducing what was owed.
rows.anchor: وروى الوالبي عنه: ولستم بآخذي هذا الردي لو كان لأحدكم على الآخر حق

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah say buyers would only accept such produce in the market at a reduced price, not the price of good produce.
rows.anchor: الحسن وقتادة: لو وجدتموه بياعا في السوق ما أخذتموه بسعر الجيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ adds that a person would accept the defective item as a gift only with embarrassment and annoyance; people should not offer God what they reject for themselves.
rows.anchor: فكيف ترضون لي ما لا ترضون لأنفسكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recipients of zakat share in the owner's property: when all of it is good, they share in the good; if it is all poor quality, paying that is permissible unless the giver voluntarily improves it.
rows.anchor: أخبر الله تعالى أن أهل السهمان شركاء رب المال في ماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is independent of people's spending and charity, and praised in His acts.
rows.anchor: واعلموا أن الله غني عن نفقاتكم وصدقاتكم حميد

rows.speaker: معبد بن منقذ عن أبي شريح الكعبي
rows.claim: Abū Shurayḥ al-Kaʿbī says to rebuke him as insane if people see him giving away the worst of what he owns.
rows.anchor: إذا رأيتموني أتصدق شر ما عندي فاكووني واعلموا إني مجنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “Satan promises you poverty,” the preposition bi is understood but omitted; a line of poetry illustrates the construction.
rows.anchor: أي بالفقر فحذف الباء كقول الشاعر: أمرتك الخير فافعل ما أمرت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic commonly uses waʿada for a promise of good and awʿada for a threat of harm, though either verb can occur with either object; the source cites Qurʾan and poetry.
rows.anchor: فإذا لم يذكر الخير والشر قلت في الخير: وعدته، وفي الشر: أوعدته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poverty means bad circumstances and lack of means; its two vowelings are like the two forms of ḍaʿf. The word is associated with a broken vertebra.
rows.anchor: والفقر: سوء الحال وقلة اليد، وفيه لغتان: الفقر والفقر كالضعف والضعف.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan frightens a person that charity will impoverish him and urges him to hold his wealth back; fahshāʾ here means miserliness and withholding zakat.
rows.anchor: إن الشيطان يخوفكم بالفقر ويقول للرجل أمسك مالك

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān says every Qurʾanic use of fahshāʾ means fornication except this verse.
rows.anchor: وزعم مقاتل [بن حيان] أن كل فحشاء في القرآن فهو الزنا إلا في هذه الآية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's promise means recompense: God's promise comes through inspiration and revelation, while Satan's consists of whispers and imaginings.
rows.anchor: وعد الله إلهام وتنزيل، ووعد الشيطان وساوس وتخيل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises forgiveness for sins and bounty in the form of provision and replacement; a Torah saying is cited about spending from God's provision to receive His favor.
rows.anchor: مغفرة منه لذنوبكم وفضلا أي رزقا وخلفا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī interprets wisdom as prophethood.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: هي النبوة.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah define wisdom as Qurʾanic knowledge: abrogating and abrogated, clear and ambiguous, earlier and later, lawful and unlawful.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية: علم القرآن: ناسخه ومنسوخه، ومحكمه ومتشابهه

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says wisdom is the Qurʾan and sound judgment in it; he warns believers to learn its many legal verses rather than imitate the Khārijites' misapplication of verses about the People of the Book, which led them to bloodshed, accusations, and plunder.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: القرآن والحكم فيه. وقال: في القرآن مائة وتسع آيات ناسخة ومنسوخة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vows fall into obedience and sin: a vow to God must be fulfilled, with expiation for abandoning it; a vow to Satan is fulfilled neither with performance nor expiation.
rows.anchor: والنذر نذران: نذر في الطاعة، ونذر في المعصية.

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says the masculine singular “He knows it” refers back to the nearest item, the vow; alternatively its pronoun refers to mā as in the phrase with yaʿiẓukum bihi.
rows.anchor: لأنه رده إلى الآخر منها كقوله ومن يكسب خطيئة أو إثما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoers are those who misplace spending and vows through ostentation or sin; they have no helpers to avert God's punishment. Anṣār is the plural of naṣīr.
rows.anchor: الواضعين النفقة والنذر في غير موضعها بالرياء والمعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After people asked whether public or secret charity was better, the verse says public giving is a good act; the wording faniʿmā praises this excellent deed.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنهم قالوا: يا رسول الله صدقة السر أفضل أم صدقة العلانية؟ فأنزل الله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression derives from niʿma mā, with mā joined and assimilated; its syntax is compared to “excellent is the man” before or after naming him.
rows.anchor: فأصله نعم ما فوصلت وأدغمت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads faniʿma mā as two words, preserving the original form.
rows.anchor: وكان الحسن يقرأها فنعم ما مفصولة على الأصل

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع غير ورش وعاصم برواية أبي بكر وأبو عمرو وأبو بحرية
rows.claim: These readers use the kasra-on-nūn, sukūn-on-ʿayn form faniʿmā; Abū ʿUbayd prefers it and calls it the Prophet's language, citing his phrase to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ.
rows.anchor: واختاره أبو عبيدة ذكر أنها لغة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عامر ويحيى بن ثابت والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: These readers pronounce faniʿamā with fatḥa on both nūn and ʿayn.
rows.anchor: بفتح النون والعين فيهما

rows.speaker: طلحة وابن كثير ويعقوب وأيوب
rows.claim: These readers use kasra on both nūn and ʿayn, which Abū Ḥātim prefers; the source regards all the forms as sound dialects.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة وابن كثير ويعقوب وأيوب بكسر النون والعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealing charity and giving it to the poor is better and preferable, though either public or private giving is accepted if the intention is sincere.
rows.anchor: وكل مقبول إذا كانت النية صادقة ولكن صدقة السر أفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says secret charity extinguishes the Lord's anger and sin as water extinguishes fire, and averts seventy gates of affliction.
rows.anchor: صدقة السر تطفي غضب الرب وتطفي الخطيئة كما يطفئ الماء النار

rows.speaker: حفص بن عاصم عن أبي هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet's seven groups sheltered on Judgment Day, including the person who conceals a gift so thoroughly that the other hand does not know it.
rows.anchor: ورجل تصدق بصدقة فأخفاها حتى لم تعلم يمينه ما ينفق شماله

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Shahr ibn Ḥawshab reports Ibn ʿAbbās reading yukaffir with yāʾ and nominative, meaning God forgives.
rows.anchor: أنه قرأ ويكفر بالياء والرفع على معنى يكفر الله

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وعاصم وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: These readers use the first-person plural with nominative as an independent clause: “We forgive,” with the plural expressing majesty.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وعاصم وأبو عمرو ويعقوب: بالنون ورفع الراء على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وأيوب وأبو حاتم
rows.claim: These readers use the first-person plural in the jussive, coordinating it with the jussive conditional after fa-huwa khayrun lakum.
rows.anchor: بالنون والجزم معا على الفاء التي في قوله فهو خير لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in “from your sins” is partitive, leaving believers wary because forgiveness depends on God's will; Basran grammarians instead say it cancels the whole preposition sense, meaning all sins are forgiven.
rows.anchor: أدخل (من) للتبعيض، وعلته: المشيئة ليكون العباد فيها على وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse concerns voluntary charity: obligatory zakat and prayers are better performed publicly or in congregation so others can follow and suspicion of ostentation is dispelled, while voluntary acts are best concealed.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية في صدقة التطوع لإجماع العلماء ان الزكاة المفروضة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar applies public giving to obligatory zakat and concealed giving to voluntary charity.
rows.anchor: يدل عليه ما روى عمار الذهبي عن أبي جعفر أنه قال في قوله إن تبدوا الصدقات فنعما هي قال: يعني الزكاة المفروضة

rows.speaker: معد بن سويد الكلبي
rows.claim: A report raised to the Prophet compares saying the recitation aloud or quietly to giving charity aloud or secretly.
rows.anchor: إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل عن الجهر بالقراءة والإخفاء بها

rows.speaker: كثير بن مرة عن عقبة بن عامر
rows.claim: ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir reports that quiet Qurʾan recitation resembles concealed charity and loud recitation resembles public charity.
rows.anchor: المسر بالقرآن كالمسر بالصدقة والجاهر بالقرآن كالجاهر بالصدقة

rows.speaker: علي بن طلحة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says secret voluntary charity is seventy times better than public voluntary charity, while public obligatory charity is twenty-five times better than concealed obligatory charity; the distinction applies to all obligations and voluntary acts.
rows.anchor: جعل الله عز وجل صدقة التطوع في السر تفضل علانيتها بسبعين ضعفا

rows.speaker: يمان
rows.claim: Yamān interprets the spending as Abū Sufyān and his companions' expenditures at Badr and Uḥud in opposition to the Messenger.
rows.anchor: قال يمان: يعني نفقات أبي سفيان وأصحابه ببدر وأحد على عداوة الرسول

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says it means the lower-ranking Jews' spending on their leaders and scholars, including Kaʿb and his companions.
rows.anchor: مقاتل: يعني نفقة سفلة اليهود على علمائهم ورؤسائهم كعب وأصحابه.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid takes the verse to mean all unbelievers' worldly spending and charity.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: يعني جميع نفقات الكفار في الدنيا وصدقاتهم.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says ṣirr is the killing hot simoom, from which God created the jinn; Ibn Kaysān says it is a wind with sound and fire, while most commentators say it is intense cold.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني السموم الحارة التي تقتل، ومنه خلق الله الجان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who wronged themselves are the crop's owners, because they disbelieved, sinned, and withheld what was due to God.
rows.anchor: زرع قوم لموا أنفسهم بالكفر والمعصية ومنع حق الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unbelievers' spending is like a cold wind or fire destroying a crop: its hoped-for benefit disappears when needed, and God has not wronged them; they wrong themselves by disbelief, sin, and withholding God's due.
rows.anchor: مثل نفقات الكفار في بطلانها وذهابها وعدم منفعتها وقت حاجتهم إليها

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة عن رسول الله
rows.claim: A report from Abū Umāmah says the Prophet identified the people meant by “do not take intimates besides yourselves” as the Khārijites.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أمامة عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله: يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تتخذوا بطانة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the warning concerned a Muslim who kept close relations with Jews through kinship, friendship, alliance, neighborhood, and foster ties; the verse forbade such intimacy for fear of their harm.
rows.anchor: كان رجل من المسلمين يواصل رجالا من اليهود لما كان بينهم من القرابة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the verse concerned believers who befriended and mixed with hypocrites; it prohibits taking confidants and allies from outside the faith community.
rows.anchor: نزلت في قوم من المؤمنين كانوا يصادفون المنافقين ويخالطونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Biṭānah is a verbal noun used as a common noun for one or many, male or female; a confidant is like the garment lining next to the body because he knows private matters.
rows.anchor: والبطانة: مصدر يوضع موضع الاسم فسمي بها الواحد والاثنان والجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reason for the prohibition is that they will spare no effort to corrupt and harm the believers; la yaʾlūkum khabālan means they will not fall short.
rows.anchor: لا يألونكم خبالا، أي لا يقصرون ولا يتركون عهدهم وطاقتهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A line attributed to Ibn Masʿūd uses the phrase “you did not fail to do good” to illustrate lā taʾlū; Imruʾ al-Qays likewise uses lā āl for not falling short in pursuit.
rows.anchor: ولم تأل عن خير لأخرى باديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khabāl means harm and corruption, as in the verse about hypocrites adding khabāl; grammatically, khabālan can be a second object, a cognate accusative, or a noun with an omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: الخبال: الشر والفساد، قال الله تعالى: لو خرجوا فيكم ما زادوكم إلا خبالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They wish the believers harm, trouble, sin, and destruction.
rows.anchor: ودوا ما عنتم أي تمنوا ضركم وشركم وإثمكم وهلاككم

rows.speaker: العامة
rows.claim: The common reading has feminine tāʾ in “hostility has appeared,” agreeing with al-baghḍāʾ; its signs are insults and defamation, or revealing believers' secrets to polytheists, like the phrase “you will know them by their speech.”
rows.anchor: قد ظهرت امارة العداوة من أفواههم بالشتيمة والوقيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The enmity and treachery concealed in their hearts are greater than what appears outwardly; God has clarified the signs for those who reason.
rows.anchor: وما تخفي صدورهم من العداوة والخيانة أكبر أعظم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports two enigmatic sayings of the Prophet against seeking illumination from polytheists and engraving Arabic; al-Ḥasan explains them as prohibiting consultation and engraving Muhammad's name on rings.
rows.anchor: فحدثهم ذات يوم وقال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «لا تستضيئوا بنار المشركين

rows.speaker: عياض الأشعري
rows.claim: ʿIyāḍ al-Ashʿarī reports that ʿUmar rebuked Abū Mūsā for employing a Christian scribe, citing the prohibition on taking non-Muslim confidants and the ban on taking Jews and Christians as allies.
rows.anchor: أما سمعت قول الله تعالى يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تتخذوا بطانة من دونكم

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā defended the arrangement by saying the scribe had his religion and he had his, and that he would not honor, elevate, or draw close those God had degraded and distanced.
rows.anchor: وفد أبو موسى الأشعري إلى عمر بن الخطاب، فقال: إن عندنا كاتبا حافظا نصرانيا

rows.speaker: مجاهد والكلبي والواقدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, and al-Wāqidī say the Prophet walked from ʿĀʾishah's home to Uḥud and arranged his companions in straight ranks, telling those whose chests protruded to step back.
rows.anchor: غدا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من منزل عائشة فمشى على رجليه إلى أحد

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق والسدي عن رجالهما
rows.claim: A report says the polytheists arrived at Uḥud on Wednesday; the Prophet consulted his companions and for the first time summoned ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy.
rows.anchor: على ما ذكر محمد بن إسحاق والسدي عن رجالهما. يوم الأربعاء، فلما سمع رسول الله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي بن سلول وأكثر الأنصار
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and most Anṣār urged staying inside Medina: they said departures had brought Muslim losses, while invaders entering the city could be fought by men and attacked from above by women and children.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله، أقم بالمدينة ولا تخرج إليهم، فو الله ما خرجنا منها إلى عدو قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet liked this counsel to stay in Medina and fight in its alleys if the enemy entered.
rows.anchor: فأعجب رسول الله بهذا الرأي

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابه
rows.claim: Some companions urged an outward march so the enemy would not think the Muslims afraid or weak.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله أخرج بنا إلى هذه الأكلب لا يرون إنا جبنا

rows.speaker: النعمان بن مالك الأنصاري
rows.claim: Al-Nuʿmān ibn Mālik asked not to be denied Paradise and vowed to enter it because he testified to God's oneness and would not flee battle; the Prophet affirmed him, and he was killed that day.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله لا تحرمني الجنة فو الذي بعثك بالحق لأدخلن الجنة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet interpreted his dream of cows as good, a notch in his sword as defeat, and putting his hand into a strong coat of mail as Medina; he recommended staying there.
rows.anchor: رأيت في منامي بقرا فأولتها خيرا، ورأيت في ذباب سيفي ثلما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Muslims who fought at Badr and were later honored with martyrdom at Uḥud repeatedly pressed the Prophet to march out; after he put on armor they regretted opposing him while revelation came.
rows.anchor: فلم يزالوا برسول الله من حبهم للقاء القوم حتى دخل رسول الله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When the companions apologized and told him to do as he judged best, the Prophet said that a prophet who puts on his armor does not remove it before fighting.
rows.anchor: « [إنه ليس لنبي] أن يلبس [لامته] أن يضعها حتى يقاتل»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thaʿlabī counts twenty-six expeditions personally led by the Prophet, beginning with Waddān (al-Abwāʾ) and ending with Tabūk, and lists their names and locations.
rows.anchor: جميع ما غزا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بنفسه ست وعشرون غزوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the Prophet fought in nine campaigns: Badr, Uḥud, the Trench, Qurayẓah, al-Muṣṭaliq, Banū Liḥyān, Khaybar, the conquest of Mecca, and Ḥunayn, with dates from 2 to 8 AH.
rows.anchor: قاتل منها في تسع غزوات: غزوة بدر الكبرى، وهو يوم الجمعة السابع عشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr was the first campaign in which the Prophet personally fought, while Tabūk was the last expedition he personally led.
rows.anchor: فأول غزوة غزاها بنفسه وقاتل فيها بدر وآخرها تبوك
